deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the front flyleaf of Gauss's copy of Christian Leiste, 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel 1790), so the notes most likely date from his student years (about 1791-1796). The page has three blocks.

(A) Integrating falling factorials. Write x^(n) = x(x-1)...(x-n+1); Gauss's vinculum notation x.x-1.x-2 means this product. He integrates polynomials and re-expresses each result in the falling-factorial basis.
(1) ∫x dx = x²/2 = ½x^(2) + ½x. This holds because x² = x(x-1) + x.
(2) ∫x(x-1) dx = x³/3 - x²/2. Using x³ = x^(3) + 3x^(2) + x (Stirling numbers of the second kind) and x² = x^(2) + x, this equals ⅓x^(3) + ½x^(2) - ⅙x, as written.
(3) The left-hand side of the third line is not written. My reconstruction: it is ∫x(x-1)(x-2) dx = x⁴/4 - x³ + x². Using x⁴ = x^(4) + 6x^(3) + 7x^(2) + x, this gives ¼x^(4) + ½x^(3) - ¼x^(2) + ¼x, which matches the page.
The purpose appears to be connecting the integral calculus of powers with the difference calculus of factorial powers. This is the standard route between Σ and ∫ (Newton/Stirling interpolation, Euler-Maclaurin).

(B) Sums of reciprocal squares split by residue classes.
- 1 - 1/9 + 1/25 - 1/49 + ... = 0.916. This is the constant now called Catalan's constant, G = 0.9159656...
- ζ(2) = Σ1/n² = π²/6 ≈ 1.6.
- Odd squares: Σ1/(2k+1)² = π²/8 ≈ 1.2.
- Even squares: Σ1/(2k)² = π²/24 ≈ 0.4.
- Modulo 3: the classes 1 and 2 mod 3 are left blank. These sums are ψ'(1/3)/9 and ψ'(2/3)/9 (equivalently they involve the Clausen value Cl₂(2π/3)) and have no elementary closed form. The class 0 mod 3 gives Σ1/(3k)² = π²/54 ≈ 0.18.
- Modulo 4:
  - Σ1/(4k+1)² = 1.074833. This equals π²/16 + G/2 = 1.07483307...
  - Σ1/(4k+2)² = π²/32.
  - Σ1/(4k+3)² = 0.15886... (a crossed-out value precedes it). This equals π²/16 - G/2 = 0.15886748...
  - Σ1/(4k)² = π²/96.
The two odd classes are obtained by adding and subtracting the alternating sum G to and from the odd-square sum π²/8 and halving. The six correct digits of 1.074833 imply G was known to about 0.9159656, not just the 0.916 written.

(C) The Gaussian integral, noted 'Aus La Place S. ...': ∫_0^∞ e^{-t²} dt is written as '= 2√π'. The correct value is √π/2.
The scattered scribbles e^{-tt-uu} dt du, e^{-rr-ss}, 1/(1+tt), and 'dt/dt = 2/(1+tt)' (probably du/dt or similar) indicate an attempt to reproduce Laplace's double-integral evaluation. Squaring the integral gives ∫∫e^{-(t²+u²)} dt du. Laplace's substitution u = ts reduces this to ∫_0^∞ ds/(1+s²) = π/2, giving I² = π/4. Polar coordinates (r, φ) give the same result.
The fragments 'dd φ/dt² = -2t' and 'e^{-φφ+2φ...}' are too fragmentary to reconstruct with certainty.
errors: The value of ∫_0^∞ e^{-t²} dt is written as '2√π'; the correct value is ½√π. This may be a slip, or a ½ that the transcription and image render poorly.
In the third integration line the left-hand side ∫x(x-1)(x-2)dx is omitted; the right-hand side is correct for that integrand.
The decimal approximations 1,6 / 1,2 / 0.4 / 0,18 are truncations (1.6449, 1.2337, 0.4112, 0.1828), not roundings. They are fine as rough values.
All other identities and values check out, including 1.074833 and 0.15886, which are correct to the digits given.

results.what: Integrals of x and of the falling factorials x(x-1), x(x-1)(x-2), expressed in the falling-factorial basis
results.modern_name: Conversion between power and falling-factorial bases (Stirling numbers of the second kind); umbral/difference calculus

results.usually_credited_to: Euler (numerical value, 18th c.); named after Catalan (1865)

results.what: Σ1/n² = π²/6, odd squares π²/8, even squares π²/24, multiples of 3 π²/54, classes 2 and 0 mod 4 π²/32 and π²/96

results.modern_name: Hurwitz zeta values ζ(2,1/4)/16 and ζ(2,3/4)/16, expressed via Catalan's constant

results.what: ∫_0^∞ e^{-t²} dt via the double integral e^{-t²-u²} (Laplace's method)

deep.surprise_reason: These are student exercises recapitulating Euler and Laplace: the Basel-type sums split by residue class, Catalan's constant, the factorial-power integrals, and the Gaussian integral. They are mainly interesting biographically, showing early contact with Laplace and the Gaussian integral and an accurate numerical G. Nothing here is a new result.

transcription_corrections: The third integration line lacks its left-hand side on the page. It should be understood as ∫x.x-1.x-2.dx; it is not a continuation of the second line.
The heading '∫ x, ...' at the top is a struck-out false start.
'Aus La Place S.' is likely 'Aus La Place S[eite]' or an abbreviated reference to a Laplace memoir; the reading is uncertain.
The written value '= 2√π' should mathematically be ½√π. Check whether the stroke before √π is a ½.
'dt/dt = 2/(1+tt)' is almost certainly a different differential, probably du/dt or dφ/dt; the scribbles near it belong to an attempted double-integral derivation.
The isolated '1 =' in the left margin and the marginal fragments are unrelated stray marks.
